form: Le Tu7kwemínem te Melmac (The Melmac Salesman)

The story is based on reminiscences of the author’s family buying dishes from a Melmac salesman in the fifties. It provides an opportunity for language learners of Secwepemctsin to note the use of the applicative suffix within a narrative context, as well as other aspects of word morphology.2

gloss: Interior Salish, the language of the story

form: Melmac is the name of a kind of plastic dinnerware which was created with the use of melamine in the 1940’s, and became popular in the 1950’s.

The author, a native speaker and instructor of Secwepemctsín (Shuswap), used her own writing to track the frequency and range of use of applicative constructions in Secwepemctsin in a course-based literature review of applicatives (Mithun, 1999; Mchombo, 1998; Payne, 1997; and Kiyosawa, 2004). The applicative suffix -min/-men appears in the title and in examples (9), (21), (23), (29), (32), (37), (39,) (40) and (42). Morpheme-by-morpheme glosses were independently provided by Dwight Gardiner and Susan Russell, and then combined and adapted by Henry Davis, who takes final responsibility for the morpheme-by-morpheme breakdown given here. Note that the particular level of analysis given here reflects the use of this text as a teaching tool in language classes; more detailed analyses are possible.

“I’m selling the absolute best plates available around this part of the country.”
“Will your parents have a look at them?”
Tsútsen: “W7ec re élkstes te logging camp
“My father is working in the logging camp”, I said.
He was asked by my mother to come into our kitchen
so we could look at his plates.
He brought his bag into the kitchen.
Then he took his dishes out of his bag.
There were two colours: yellow and a mixed green set -
Then he said: “These plates don’t ever break!”
“You can’t break it no matter what you do with it”.
Then he began showing us exactly how strong the material was.
Mtseq’míns re nek’u7 te tsk’pupcw nxlílep ell
He threw one bowl onto the floor and said:
“Even if something is heavy it won’t smash it to smithereens… Watch this.”
He jumped onto the bowl and smashed it to bits.
The man blushed and said: “I didn’t mean to do that
or want it to smash up and dirty up your floor for you.”
le túpemt te tsk’pupcw te xlílep.
I brought the broom and swept up the broken bowl off the floor.

“We won’t buy the plates today, maybe sometime later”.
Then the salesman took all of his wares and put them away.
Then he left, still smiling as he left.
I think he was embarrassed about breaking the bowl.
My mum really wanted the plates
but we had no money to buy them.
“If I were stronger I would be able to work somewhere.”

It wasn’t a long time after that, we heard about my aunt Suzy.
Mtéwm ekwe tek syelyélt tek melmac
She had bought some plates from the melmac salesman.
Ell ta7 cú7tsem k sq’7est.s tlri7
And it wasn’t long after that
my mum asked me to visit my aunt Suzy
to ask her how she was able to get the plates.
Seséle nke put tek mile re mútes re Suzy
Suzy lived about two miles away.
So then I rushed off for there.
I was told not to stay until it was after sundown.
My mum wanted me to ask her:

“How much did she pay each month?”

When it was fall I returned to Residential School in Kamloops.
She had not yet got any melmac dishes on credit.
Nek’welltyénecwem lu7 tlri7 le pelqíq’elc wen

I saw my Mum’s melmac dishes in her cupboard.
Mtéwm enke te kwalt te syelyélt.
She must have bought the yellow plates.
When I saw my Mum’s plates
she told me she was helped by my older sister Edith.
“She wrote for me everything I wanted…I was really happy.”
